prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 physiology is the clearest case of a specific discovery that changed both a research field and clinical practice: from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect to an identified active peptide and its actions, and onward to long-acting agonists that now treat type 2 diabetes and obesity with documented cardiovascular and renal benefit. All six of us ranked it first or second, which tells us about breadth of agreement but is not the argument; the argument is that the mechanism is stable, independently confirmed in large outcome trials, and the impact is measurable in millions of patients. A physiology-centred trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov keeps the prize anchored in the discovery of the hormone's biology rather than in a product.
statement.case_against: Credit allocation is the real weakness. Four people are credited and only three can be named, so either Mojsov or Knudsen is excluded. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1 form is contested in the literature, with Habener and others outside the credited list, and I cannot settle that from the supplied text. Dropping Knudsen risks being read as ignoring the drug-development step that actually produced the medicines, while including her shifts the prize toward industrial development and leaves the discovery of the active peptide underrepresented.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, valuing the unbroken line from hormone biology to long-acting liraglutide and semaglutide, and treats Mojsov's priority as a credit problem.
responses.response: I take the unbroken-line argument seriously, and I accept that the clinical story is incomplete without long-acting analogues. But my view of the prize as recognising a discovery with a discernible change in the field points to the physiology and the identification of the active peptide as the core, with the drug design a consequence of it. I would keep Mojsov over Knudsen unless the priority evidence against her proves stronger than the opening ballots suggest. I do concede that this is a judgement and that your trio is defensible; the contested nature of Mojsov's credit is the argument that most moves me towards your side.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also names Knudsen alongside Drucker and Holst, and asks whether the prize should reward basic physiology only or include industrial drug development.
responses.response: Your question about physiology versus drug development is the right one, and it is the main thing separating our configurations. I would resist letting the clinical weight of the drugs decide credit for the discovery itself, and I note that your own ranking places CAR-T (B019) third, where the same tension between concept, engineering and clinical proof arises with an incomplete credit list. If we do include Knudsen, I would want the citation to say plainly that it recognises the translation to long-acting agonists.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response (Walter, Mori) first as a conceptually original and mechanistically complete signalling pathway with a clean two-person attribution, and GLP-1 second.
responses.response: I agree that B032 has the cleanest attribution of any shortlisted candidate and the discovery is mature and fundamental. My reservation, which I also had in my own opening ranking at fourth place, is that the link from the pathway to medicine is indirect, and credit for the PERK, ATF6 and integrated stress response arms lies partly outside Walter and Mori. I do not think that cleanliness outweighs the scale of the GLP-1 effect, but I regard B032 as a serious alternative and would be comfortable with it if GLP-1 credit cannot be resolved.

responses.point: Linnarsson treats Knudsen's role as distinct from the core discovery, favours a physiology-centred trio and notes the Mojsov priority dispute is unverified.
responses.response: We agree on the structure, and I share your concern that priority claims are unverified. Where I would qualify your position is that an unresolved priority dispute is a reason for the committee to examine the primary literature carefully, not to default to the cleanest alternative; if Mojsov's role fails that scrutiny, I would prefer to revisit the trio rather than abandon the field.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should be the third name, which depends on priority evidence for the active GLP-1 form that I cannot verify from the supplied text.
Whether the committee wants to credit drug development alongside physiology.
How to weigh CAR-T (B019), whose credited names omit the originators of the chimeric receptor concept, against GLP-1 if the credit dispute cannot be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B043, B019 or B032 from my profile. My research on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap, and the co-authorship history with Ronald Evans is unrelated to any shortlisted credited name. I note for transparency that I have co-authored with colleagues on this committee (Svenningsson and, once, El Manira), which does not by itself require recusal.
